name: Apollo 11 Eagle Lunar Module Descent Stage
statusDescription: The descent stage has no working systems. It stays at Tranquility Base as a permanent marker of the first crewed Moon landing. Eagle's ascent stage was not left on the surface (see uncertainties).
landingSite: Tranquility Base, southern Mare Tranquillitatis (Sea of Tranquility)
description: The lower half of the Apollo 11 Lunar Module. Its four legs and landing engine carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin down to the Moon.
missionPurpose: NASA needed a vehicle that could land two astronauts, support them on the surface and then serve as a launch pad for the trip back to lunar orbit.
missionStory: Eagle touched down on 20 July 1969. When the astronauts left on 21 July, the descent stage stayed behind as their launch platform and then as a monument. It is far too small to see from Earth, but NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter later photographed it from lunar orbit, where it shows up as a bright spot with a long shadow at low Sun angles.

scientificLegacy.title: First crewed landing documented from orbit
scientificLegacy.explanation: Orbital images of the site let scientists and the public see the real hardware, footprint trails and instruments where the first human visit took place.

scientificLegacy.title: Part of a larger Apollo 11 science site
scientificLegacy.explanation: The crew also left a small seismometer and a passive laser reflector nearby. The reflector is a separate object that scientists can still use for Earth-Moon distance measurements; it is not one of the 25 records in this collection.

name: Apollo 12 Intrepid Lunar Module Descent Stage
statusDescription: Passive hardware. It sits on the Ocean of Storms close to the Apollo 12 science station and the older Surveyor 3 lander.
landingSite: Ocean of Storms (Oceanus Procellarum), near the Surveyor 3 landing site
description: The lower half of Lunar Module Intrepid. Its landing was aimed at a precise spot near a lander that had already been on the Moon for two and a half years.
missionPurpose: Apollo 12 was meant to show that Apollo could land at a chosen point, not just in a broad landing zone.
missionStory: Intrepid landed on 19 November 1969 within walking distance of Surveyor 3. Astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked to the old lander and removed parts of it for study. Intrepid's descent stage stayed behind; a NASA site image shows the descent stage, the science station, Surveyor 3 and the astronauts' trails in one frame.

scientificLegacy.title: Proof of precision landing
scientificLegacy.explanation: Landing near Surveyor 3 showed that later Apollo missions could aim for small, scientifically interesting targets.

scientificLegacy.title: A rare view of hardware aging on the Moon
scientificLegacy.explanation: Having Intrepid, an ALSEP station and Surveyor 3 in one place lets researchers compare how materials of different ages look in the Moon's harsh environment.

name: Apollo 14 Antares Lunar Module Descent Stage
statusDescription: Passive hardware at the Fra Mauro landing site. NASA's orbiter has photographed it together with the Apollo 14 science station and astronaut tracks.
description: The lower half of Lunar Module Antares, which carried Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell to the Fra Mauro region.
missionPurpose: After Apollo 13 failed to land, Apollo 14 returned to the same target area: rocky terrain believed to hold material thrown out by a huge impact.
missionStory: Antares landed on 5 February 1971. Shepard and Mitchell set up a science station and made two walks, using a hand-pulled equipment cart. Orbiter images show the descent stage and the station joined by a trail of footprints.

scientificLegacy.title: A recovery mission that succeeded
scientificLegacy.explanation: Apollo 14 achieved the goals Apollo 13 could not, and returned samples from a region of great interest to lunar geologists.

scientificLegacy.title: Orbital images show human activity
scientificLegacy.explanation: LRO pictures of the Antares site show the descent stage, instruments and astronaut paths, helping the public connect the data to a real place.

name: Apollo 15 Falcon Lunar Module Descent Stage
statusDescription: Passive hardware at Hadley-Apennine, left near the Apollo 15 science station and the first Lunar Roving Vehicle.
description: The lower half of Lunar Module Falcon, a longer-stay lander that carried David Scott and James Irwin plus the first Moon rover.
missionPurpose: Apollo 15 was the first of the longer Apollo 'J' missions, built for more time on the surface, more science and a rover.
missionStory: Falcon landed on 30 July 1971 beside Hadley Rille and the Apennine mountains. The astronauts ranged much farther than earlier crews because they could drive. When they left on 2 August, the descent stage, science station and rover stayed behind.

scientificLegacy.title: A new level of exploration
scientificLegacy.explanation: Apollo 15 showed how a longer stay and a rover could greatly widen the area a crew could study.

scientificLegacy.title: Part of a connected set of left-behind tools
scientificLegacy.explanation: The Falcon site holds a science station, a rover and a lander stage, so it tells a fuller story than any one object.

name: Apollo 16 Orion Lunar Module Descent Stage
statusDescription: Passive hardware in the Descartes Highlands, the only Apollo landing in true lunar highlands terrain.
description: The lower half of Lunar Module Orion, which carried John Young and Charles Duke into the Moon's old, heavily cratered highlands.
missionPurpose: Scientists wanted samples from the highlands, which are older than the dark plains, and expected some of them to be volcanic.
missionStory: Orion landed on 21 April 1972 and the crew made three moonwalks, using the rover. The results surprised many researchers because the highland rocks did not turn out to be mainly volcanic. Orion's descent stage, a science station and the rover remain at the site.

scientificLegacy.title: A lesson in testing assumptions
scientificLegacy.explanation: Apollo 16 showed that an expected explanation can be wrong, which is a central idea in science.

scientificLegacy.title: Samples from the ancient crust
scientificLegacy.explanation: Highland rocks gathered here help researchers study how the Moon's early crust formed and was battered by impacts.

name: Apollo 17 Challenger Lunar Module Descent Stage
statusDescription: Passive hardware at Taurus-Littrow, left at the end of the last crewed Moon landing so far.
description: The lower half of Lunar Module Challenger, which carried Eugene Cernan and geologist Harrison Schmitt to a valley between mountains.
missionPurpose: Apollo 17 was the final Apollo landing, and the only one to carry a professional scientist-astronaut.
missionStory: Challenger landed on 11 December 1972. The crew made three moonwalks and used the rover to reach craters and hills far from the lander. The descent stage, the rover and a science station stayed behind. NASA's orbiter has since photographed the site at high resolution.

scientificLegacy.title: The end of a program, still visible
scientificLegacy.explanation: Sharper LRO images of the Apollo 17 site show the stage and equipment, and mark the place of the last Apollo visit.

scientificLegacy.title: A scientist on the Moon
scientificLegacy.explanation: Having a geologist on the crew shows how trained scientists can add value to exploration, a lesson for future missions.

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
statusDescription: Parked at Hadley-Apennine after three moonwalks. It has no working crew or controllers; it is passive hardware.
description: The first battery-powered Moon buggy, folded into the side of the Lunar Module and driven by David Scott and James Irwin.
missionPurpose: To let astronauts travel beyond walking range and carry tools and samples.
missionStory: The rover made its first drive on 31 July 1971. The Apollo 15 crew drove about 27.9 kilometres in total, much farther than any walking crew could safely go from the lander. When they left, the rover was parked for good.

scientificLegacy.title: It expanded how far crews could explore
scientificLegacy.explanation: A source on the National Archives exhibit notes that rovers made many of the major Apollo 15-17 discoveries possible by extending the crews' range.

scientificLegacy.title: Proof that electric vehicles can work on the Moon
scientificLegacy.explanation: The rover operated in vacuum and low gravity for three days, an important engineering test for later lunar vehicles.

name: Apollo 16 Lunar Roving Vehicle
statusDescription: Parked in the Descartes Highlands after three moonwalks. Passive hardware.
description: The second Moon buggy, used by John Young and Charles Duke to cross hilly highland terrain.
missionPurpose: To carry the crew and samples to the highland sites that scientists had chosen.
missionStory: The rover began operations in April 1972. Young and Duke drove it to craters and slopes in the Descartes area. The crew drove roughly 26.7 kilometres in total (see uncertainties) before leaving it behind.

scientificLegacy.title: Mobility in rougher terrain
scientificLegacy.explanation: The highlands are hillier than the Apollo 15 plains, so this rover tested the vehicle in more demanding terrain.

scientificLegacy.title: Samples from a wider area
scientificLegacy.explanation: Driving allowed the crew to collect rocks from several locations instead of just near the lander.

name: Apollo 12 ALSEP
statusDescription: NASA commanded all ALSEP stations off on 30 September 1977, mainly because of budget reasons. The hardware remains at the site and its data are still available for study.
description: The first full Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package, left by Pete Conrad and Alan Bean. It ran on a radioisotope power unit and sent its data to Earth by radio.
missionPurpose: To measure the Moon's quakes, magnetic field and the particles around it for much longer than one crew's stay.
missionStory: The station started sending data on 19 November 1969, the day of the landing. It was designed to run for about a year, but NASA says the Apollo stations ran for up to about eight years. Its seismometer joined those of later missions to form the first network of seismometers on another world.

scientificLegacy.title: A working science network
scientificLegacy.explanation: NASA reports that the seismometers at Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16 operated together as a seismic network.

scientificLegacy.title: Data still used today
scientificLegacy.explanation: The measurements were archived, including by NASA's Planetary Data System, and continue to be reused by researchers.

missionStory: Deployed on 5 February 1971, this station had a troubled engineering history, according to a NASA news release written when the stations were turned off. Even so, it kept working until the 1977 shutdown. Orbital images show the station connected to the lander by footprints.

scientificLegacy.title: Longer record than the crew's stay
scientificLegacy.explanation: The station kept sending data for years, giving a much longer record than a short visit could.

scientificLegacy.title: Added a third seismic point
scientificLegacy.explanation: Together with Apollo 12 and later stations, it helped scientists locate quakes and impacts.

name: Apollo 15 ALSEP
statusDescription: Commanded off with the other ALSEP stations on 30 September 1977. It remains at Hadley-Apennine.
description: The Apollo 15 science station, set up by David Scott and James Irwin near the lander. It was the first one deployed by a crew that also had a rover.

scientificLegacy.title: Extended the seismic network

scientificLegacy.title: Documented long-term lunar conditions
scientificLegacy.explanation: Its long operation gave scientists a record of the Moon's environment across many lunar days.

name: Surveyor 1
statusDescription: Surveyor 1 survived its first lunar night, sent more data afterwards, then fell silent. Its last contact is given as 7 January 1967 (some sources give 8 January because of time zones).
landingSite: Ocean of Storms, near the crater Flamsteed
description: NASA's first soft landing on the Moon and the first American spacecraft to land on another world, on its first try.
missionPurpose: To show that a spacecraft could land softly and to learn whether the Moon's surface could hold up a heavy lander.
missionStory: Surveyor 1 touched down on 2 June 1966, four months after the Soviet Luna 9. Its three crushable footpads sank only slightly into the soil, which was good news for Apollo planners. It sent back thousands of pictures and lasted far past its first lunar night.

scientificLegacy.title: The ground could hold a lander
scientificLegacy.explanation: The small footpad sinkage gave NASA direct evidence that a crewed lander could be supported.

scientificLegacy.title: First close-up views of the Moon's surface
scientificLegacy.explanation: Its television camera sent back thousands of images used to plan later landings.

scientificLegacy.explanation: Scientists could examine how spacecraft materials changed after about 2.5 years on the surface.

name: Surveyor 5
statusDescription: Operations ended in December 1967 (date from a secondary table); the spacecraft fell silent as it lost power.
landingSite: Mare Tranquillitatis (Sea of Tranquility), about 25 km from where Apollo 11 later landed

missionStory: Surveyor 5 landed on 11 September 1967, on a steep slope after a difficult descent. Its soil analysis suggested the surface material resembles basalt. It also sent back about 19,000 images.

scientificLegacy.title: First on-site soil chemistry
scientificLegacy.explanation: The alpha-scattering instrument gave a direct measurement of the lunar soil, found to be basaltic.

scientificLegacy.title: Scouting for Apollo 11
scientificLegacy.explanation: Landing in the Sea of Tranquility gave NASA information about the region Apollo 11 later visited.

name: Surveyor 6
statusDescription: Contact ended in December 1967. NASA treats it as the end of the mission.
description: A robotic lander that made the first liftoff from another world, a short hop on its own engines.
missionPurpose: To photograph the area, analyze soil and test whether a spacecraft could lift off and move after landing.
missionStory: Surveyor 6 landed on 10 November 1967 (9 November in US time). On 17 November it fired its engines for a short hop to a spot a few metres away, and took stereo pictures of its original footprints. Contact ended in mid-December.

scientificLegacy.title: First hop on another world
scientificLegacy.explanation: The short engine hop showed a lander could lift off the Moon, a key step toward Apollo ascent stages.

scientificLegacy.title: Stereo views of the surface
scientificLegacy.explanation: Pictures from before and after the hop showed how the soil responded to engine thrust and footpads.

name: Viking 1 Lander
statusDescription: On 11 November 1982 a faulty command from Earth overwrote antenna-pointing data, and contact was lost. JPL announced in April 1983 that attempts to restore contact had ended.
description: The first successful long-term lander on Mars, powered by a radioisotope generator. It was later named the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station.
missionPurpose: To photograph Mars from the surface, study its weather and soil, and test the ground for signs of life.
missionStory: Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976 and sent the first picture taken from the surface of Mars. It was designed to last about 90 days, but worked for more than six years. In 2006 NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it on the surface.

scientificLegacy.title: Long-term weather record
scientificLegacy.explanation: Years of readings on temperature, pressure and wind gave the first long record of Martian weather.

scientificLegacy.title: A first test for life on Mars
scientificLegacy.explanation: Its experiments looked for biological activity; results were ambiguous and still debated, which shaped the design of later missions.

scientificLegacy.title: Seasonal change at the surface
scientificLegacy.explanation: Repeat photos revealed frost and seasonal changes, showing Mars is an active place.

scientificLegacy.title: Two sites instead of one

name: Sojourner Rover
statusDescription: The Pathfinder lander stopped sending signals after 27 September 1997. Sojourner depended on the lander to talk to Earth, so its mission ended too.
landingSite: Ares Vallis, Chryse Planitia (the lander was named Carl Sagan Memorial Station)
description: A microwave-oven-sized, six-wheeled rover and the first wheeled vehicle to drive on Mars.
missionPurpose: To prove that a small, low-cost rover could drive and analyze rocks on Mars.
missionStory: Sojourner rolled off the Pathfinder lander on 6 July 1997. It used a small instrument to measure the chemistry of rocks nicknamed Barnacle Bill and Yogi. It was designed for about a week but operated for many weeks.

scientificLegacy.title: Rovers work on Mars
scientificLegacy.explanation: Sojourner showed that small rovers can drive, take measurements and survive on the surface, paving the way for Spirit, Opportunity and later rovers.

scientificLegacy.title: Rock chemistry from a first rover
scientificLegacy.explanation: Its measurements gave scientists a first on-the-spot look at Martian rocks.

name: Spirit Rover
statusDescription: Spirit's last contact was on 22 March 2010. NASA kept trying to reach it until May 2011, when the mission was declared over.

scientificLegacy.title: Past water at Gusev
scientificLegacy.explanation: Spirit found minerals that formed in the presence of water, hot springs or steam vents.

scientificLegacy.title: A strong overachiever
scientificLegacy.explanation: It was planned for 90 sols and operated for about 2,210 sols.

name: Opportunity Rover

description: The second of the twin Mars Exploration Rovers. It drove farther than any other rover and lasted nearly 15 years.

missionStory: Opportunity landed on 25 January 2004 (24 January in US time). It was planned to last about 90 days. It eventually drove more than 28 miles, and ended in Perseverance Valley. NASA declared the mission complete after the rover stayed silent following the storm.

scientificLegacy.title: Past water in Meridiani
scientificLegacy.explanation: Opportunity's discoveries helped show that Mars once had liquid water.

scientificLegacy.title: A record-setting lifespan
scientificLegacy.explanation: It operated about 60 times longer than planned and set a distance record for driving on another world.

name: Phoenix Lander

scientificLegacy.title: Chemistry of the soil
scientificLegacy.explanation: It also found perchlorate salts, a discovery that affects how scientists think about life-detection tests on Mars.

scientificLegacy.title: Looking inside another planet
scientificLegacy.explanation: Seismic data revealed how Mars' interior layers are built.

scientificLegacy.explanation: Ingenuity proved that controlled flight is possible on Mars and opened the way for future aircraft.
